Latest Update: Bella Hadid’s Radical Vulnerability

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I first met Bella Hadid on a fashion shoot I was styling more than a decade ago.
  • Recent findings suggest that A few days after the Victoria’s Secret show in October, Bella and I sat down to reflect on her career so far, forgiveness and success, turning 30, and where she goes from here.
  • It has been revealed that samira Nasr: This is a full-circle moment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I first met Bella Hadid on a fashion shoot I was styling more than a decade ago. We went on to shoot several stories together, including her first major American magazine cover. On one of those shoots, she arrived upset because she had just found out she didn’t get cast in the Victoria’s Secret show. I will never forget telling Bella that one day, Victoria’s Secret would be begging her to walk for them. Cut to today, and Bella is not only one of the most in-demand models, but she opened their most recent show. When I saw her hit the runway in a beaded floral bra and matching wings, I let out a scream because I knew what that moment meant to her.

Recent findings suggest that A few days after the Victoria’s Secret show in October, Bella and I sat down to reflect on her career so far, forgiveness and success, turning 30, and where she goes from here. I have always felt connected to Bella because she, like me, is a heart-on-her-sleeve kind of gal. She is deeply vulnerable and human, and it’s what makes her one of the most compelling figures in fashion today.

It has been revealed that samira Nasr: This is a full-circle moment. On one of our first shoots together, you were really upset because you didn’t get the Victoria’s Secret show. And I said to you, “One day, they will be begging you to be in their show.” And I could tell you didn’t believe me. Your whole body shut down. And three days ago, you opened Victoria’s Secret. Holy shit.

In a recent development, bella Hadid: I still don’t believe you, to be honest. I feel like people are just AI-ing me onto the runway. I think that it’s so crazy how time passes and you still have some kind of impostor syndrome. No matter how hard you work, there’s always another girl who is more deserving, more beautiful, and has worked so hard to be able to get that spot. Ten years ago, I remember that moment too, where I never thought I would get the show, but I think that God always has a blueprint, and I truly believe at that time I wasn’t ready. I don’t think I’ve been ready until this year, to be honest. In past years, I was going to my horse-show finals in the morning, flying straight to the Victoria’s Secret show that day, doing rehearsal right before, and then pulling what we call a Bella, and Belinda comes out, and we just act. But this year, I felt really strong.

In a recent development, I have had to make a decision for myself to have boundaries with my own health. And I think it’s gotten me to this point now where I’m able to do the jobs that I do want to do with people that I love, that I can feel inspired by. And that’s truly what [working in] fashion is about: being around people you feel inspired by. Until you find that inspiration, it’s hard to go back into our industry. I think I needed a little bit of time just to be able to be like, “Let me just remember why I’m doing this again,” because I know I’m more than just a face.

SN: We don’t really support a culture of care. I have always believed that boundaries are bridges.

Industry observers note that BH: They really are. We know so many people who have been working for 30, 40, 50 years in this industry with zero boundaries. I’ve watched people over the years just get more depressed because they don’t know themselves and they don’t know who they are. And that’s how I was for 10 years, when I didn’t know what my favorite color was, what I liked to eat. I stopped listening to music. To not be able to know yourself in an industry that tells you how to be every single day is really hard.

In a recent development, SN: Going back to Victoria’s Secret, did you feel empowered, or was that your alter ego? What is her name again?

Recent findings suggest that BH: Belinda. You know what? Fortunately and unfortunately, I think it was Bella this year.

According to recent reports, SN: That’s great. I’m so happy for you.

BH: I made up my alter ego, Belinda, a long time ago to deal with the intensity of everything happening in my life. So she could deal with that, and I can deal with this, and we can do this together, which I’m realizing I should probably go to therapy about again. Belinda is the one that people are like, “Wow, this, that.”.

I have POTS [postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome], and I have a lot of PMDD [premenstrual dysphoric disorder], endometriosis, plus my Lyme and things that affect my body very deeply. Right before I walked out on the runway for my opening look, I went to go stretch and my whole clavicle completely … I don’t even know what it was. My lungs almost collapsed, and I couldn’t breathe, and then it was like, “Five, four …” So my body goes through these different motions of feeling really good and then all of a sudden crashing on me at the worst moments. I need to realize maybe my body can’t handle all that I have going on. Because I know how to walk. One thing I can do is I can strut. But it’s a lot of pressure; we all have our own insecurities. Sometimes my body just can’t connect with my brain. My brain wants to do it, and my body is like, “No, we can’t do that today.” And I’m like, “Okay, great. So let’s figure out another way.” But I think people don’t realize how much I struggle with the fatigue and the body pain, and so I just try my best.

Recent findings suggest that SN: You’ve achieved so much in your 20s. You just turned 30. What are you looking forward to in your 30s?

BH: It’s funny, today I woke up with—I wouldn’t say the word is anxiety, but this feeling of “Oh my gosh, my life is starting.” I want to get rid of what doesn’t bring me joy and bring in what does. I’ve tried to put myself in positions for work for a very long time that have made me feel out of body or like I don’t belong. Years ago, I was just grateful to get a job, and I would say yes to everything. I lacked boundaries then, but I do believe that that gave me the strength to be able to have the confidence in my own boundaries now. I’ve achieved pretty much all the goals that I wanted to when it comes to fashion as a model. And now I do want to go into other ventures to eventually get to peace and happiness and love within this universe that God has put me in.

In the next couple of years, it’s just about getting back to community, getting back to using my voice again. I got beaten down pretty heavy for a long time, which pushed me into this very substantial struggle with my physical and emotional health, which makes my brain turn off and makes me not be able to write or read. When you’re not around enough people that are like-minded, you feel really ostracized. That’s almost where I got to. Of course, I always want to speak from my heart, which I hope will never disrespect anybody, but still be able to have the confidence to speak my truth and hope that people will walk beside me along the way when it comes to that.

SN: Is there something you’re most proud of achieving?

BH: Well, first and foremost, starting [my fragrance line] Orebella was something that I truly needed for my own creativity and to be able to build community. I am not a 50/50 person. I’m an all-in type of girl. Being able to move forward into my 30s, really focusing on building the things that I’ve started—Orebella was something that I pushed so hard for since 2018, and the fact that it’s really now coming to fruition makes me so proud.

It has been revealed that when I was 17, going to my first go-see with a stylist I will not name, I was basically told I was too big to wear Saint Laurent and needed to lose a couple of pounds. And that’s when I was just a baby coming out of high school. Twelve years later, now I’m the face of Saint Laurent. I’m the face of Prada, which is incredible and insane. Times have changed so much, and the people that have come into the industry to make it a better place for us as models are so important. Not that that comment ever impacted me. I went through enough struggles with my body before that, so by the time she remarked that, I was like, “Okay, girl, I’m actually coming out of something that I dealt with very heavily when it came to my body. And now I look at food in a different way, and I love my body, and that’s okay if you think that I don’t look the way that you think I should look.”.

I just would love for everyone to think about if every day they had to walk outside and be photographed, what that would feel like, because it’s an uncomfortable feeling for anybody. My face would change so much. I would be super puffy one day, and one day I would look yellow and emaciated, and people would think I was on drugs or doing this or that. And when anybody knows about, one, hormones, just as a woman in general, and two, about immune problems and how weight fluctuates—again, I just think that there needs to be more sensitivity in our industry.

SN: I’m curious if you’ve always been this person—so sensitive, empathetic—from a little girl.

BH: I’ve always felt like my sensitivity and my openness were a disservice to myself because I felt like no one else was like me in those ways, so I shut it down. Now I realize that there is a generosity of thoughtfulness that is so much deeper than just buying somebody an expensive gift. I think sitting on the side of the street with somebody, even if you don’t have any money, is more important than just walking by without caring.

Industry observers note that SN: You’re able to access compassion when a lot of people can’t, and that is a superpower. I want to talk about style because you mentioned your archive. I remember you once mentioned you collect Gaultier. Do you still collect?

In a recent development, BH: I do collect. Behind me are bags to sell. But downstairs, I have my Gaultier dress that the atelier made. It was a Naomi Campbell dress that she had worn in one of their shows, and I was obsessed with it. I called their PR, and within a week and a half, because that dress was in a museum, I had it made and sent to Cannes, and that was that white-and-black dress that I wore on the carpet. And so, that’s here. My Coperni dress is here. I have a whole section for Virgil [Abloh].

SN: The last time I saw Virgil was with you, actually.

It has been revealed that BH: I don’t think I’ve done a real, full Fashion Month since he passed away. And Vivienne [Westwood] and Karl [Lagerfeld] passed, and I felt like all of my idols were leaving, and it felt really scary. I have all the art Virgil gave me, his letter he wrote me, his bags, his shoes he made me. And then I have my Prada area, my Cavalli area, my Bob Mackies that I’ve been collecting over the years.

BH: Hopefully for a future wedding. There are just some dresses you can’t find again. And Bob did it best.

SN: He’s an American icon. I wanted to talk to you about Cannes. You’re such a queen of Cannes now, and I look forward to seeing you there. Is it fun?

BH: This past year was fun. I felt grounded. To do the red carpet and feel, in those moments, sober and happy and healthy and strong, and go to sleep not having anxiety about going out or how I’m going to look the next day, and just being with loved ones. It did really well for me this year.

Cannes has always held a very special place in my heart. It begins long before I arrive. Working closely with designers on custom gowns, exchanging references, and watching those first sketches come to life is such a beautiful part of the experience.

This year, being there to support Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s Ben’Imana, the first Rwandan film in the official selection, was especially meaningful. It explores memory and reconciliation after the genocide against the Tutsi through women whose lives carry its legacy. That’s what I love about cinema: It brings us closer and gives stories too rarely heard the attention they deserve. You can enter a theater knowing nothing of someone’s world and leave carrying a little of it with you.

Recent findings suggest that SN: I look at you and how hard you’ve worked for so long, from our first job together. To me, it feels like you’ve achieved so much. But what does success look like for you? Do you feel you’ve achieved it?

BH: I talked to my business manager yesterday, so that made me feel a little bit more successful. But when you don’t think about the money part of it, I think success truly comes from peace within. At the end of the day, I really don’t need much. That’s why I do give back so much, because a lot of the money that I do make, I don’t feel deserving of. There are so many people in the world, whether it’s doctors or teachers, that I think deserve my pay rate a lot more than I do.

It has been revealed that from an external space, success is about how known you are, how much you make, how many times you can be on TV, how many covers you’re on, how many fashion demonstrates you do. And that is really important in our industry, especially when you’re building. But for me, I am different. Success, for me, can be living in peace, in a small town, with a man that I love, with my child, having my animals. I’ve always wanted to start a farm-to-table bakery, with flowers, and everything comes from the community. I want to do things that are fulfilling for me in my soul: having a greenhouse that I can garden in, having my glassblowing and ceramic studio, and having lots of children and being a mother. It wasn’t a dream that I’ve always had, but it’s something that now is so intense for me. My intuition is screaming so loudly at me about it.

Industry observers note that I think knowing there is a reason behind everything is so important. My sister and I donated a million dollars to Palestine last year [the donation was split between HEAL Palestine, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, World Central Kitchen, and United Nations Relief and Works Agency], which we could have never been able to do without the success that we’ve had.

According to recent reports, god gave me the platform to be able to speak about the things that I hold dearly to me. And when it comes to Palestine or Sudan or Congo or Rwanda or places that mean so much to not only myself but the people around me—to give people a voice in any capacity, that’s success for me as well. To make my family wide and far proud, or to see themselves in me, it gives me strength.

This story appears in the Winter problem of Harper’s Bazaar.

#124381. Latest Update: Artificial Sweeteners May Be Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline, Latest Study Finds

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1328 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Elle ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Artificial Sweeteners May Be Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline, Latest Study Finds

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that sugar can be quite a controversial ingredient.
  • Rachel Brief, RD, a registered dietitian nutritionist based in NYC, explains to ELLE that glucose is the brain’s primary energy source and essential for normal and healthy brain function.
  • Overall, sugar isn’t bad; however, there are several ways both regular sugar and artificial sweeteners affect brain function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sugar can be quite a controversial ingredient. Added sugars and refined versions have been linked to diabetes, obesity, and heart problems. But attempts at going the healthier route with artificial sweeteners have mixed reviews over the years because of both taste and possible long-term side effects. Now, a study by the American Academy of Neurology suggests that out of the 13,000 adults analyzed, those who consumed the most artificial sweeteners over the eight-year study period had a 62 percent faster decline in memory and thinking skills than those who consumed the least. The data means the brain aged by just over a year and a half. Experts explain what artificial sweetener use means for long-term health and whether it’s time to get rid of the sugar substitutes for good.

Rachel Brief, RD, a registered dietitian nutritionist based in NYC, explains to ELLE that glucose is the brain’s primary energy source and essential for normal and healthy brain function. However, she warns that excessive consumption of added sugars can have negative implications for long-term brain health. “Diets high in added sugar have been associated with insulin resistance, inflammation, and metabolic dysfunction, all of which may influence cognitive health over time,” she shares. “Sugar also activates the brain’s reward pathways, including dopamine signaling, which reinforces pleasurable eating experiences.”.

Overall, sugar isn’t bad; however, there are several ways both regular sugar and artificial sweeteners affect brain function. Jessica L. Zwerling, MD, director of the Montefiore Hudson Valley Center of Excellence for Alzheimer’s Disease (CEAD), shares a few of the main ones:.

Industry observers note that brief further explains that artificial sweeteners, specifically, interact with sweet-taste receptors, “Allowing us to experience sweetness without the same glucose load or caloric contribution as conventional sugar. However, their effects may extend beyond simply providing sweetness,” she notes. “Emerging research suggests that certain sweeteners may influence metabolic signaling, appetite regulation, and the gut microbiome, which plays an important role in communication between the gut and brain. We’re still learning how these interactions may influence cognitive health over time,” claims Brief.

Sources indicate that researchers from the American Academy of Neurology examined seven common artificial sweeteners used in foods and beverages: aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol, and tagatose. While the study results show an association between higher consumption and brain function, particularly memory and verbal fluency, as noted, it doesn’t prove a cause-and-effect relationship between the two.

Sources indicate that since there is insufficient evidence to establish a causal link between artificial sweeteners and deteriorating brain function, both Brief and Zwerling caution against directly making that claim. However, Zwerling indicates that other research has connected artificial sweeteners to dementia and ischemic stroke.

Industry observers note that as for the decline in brain function, Brief points out that emerging research has identified associations between higher consumption of certain sweeteners and faster declines in cognitive performance, particularly in areas such as memory and processing speed. “Potential mechanisms being explored include changes in metabolic health, insulin signaling, inflammation, and gut microbiome composition. More research is needed to understand whether these sweeteners directly contribute to cognitive changes,” she adds.

Zwerling elaborates on these potential mechanisms that may be at the root of it:.

According to recent reports, artificial sweeteners may alter the composition and function of the gut microbiome. These changes may influence inflammation. “In other words, there is a change in the communication between the gut and brain,” Zwerling explains.

In a recent development, some sweeteners may influence insulin secretion, glucose metabolism, and hormonal responses. “Insulin signaling is crucial for neuronal function, synaptic plasticity, and memory. Truly, what we eat affects how we think,” Zwerling cautions. Additionally, she notes that empirical studies have shown that consuming aspartame can lead to increased cytokine IL1β—a signaling protein in the body that regulates immune and inflammatory responses—thereby inducing systemic inflammation as well as suppression of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) alpha, another naturally occurring protein that helps coordinate immune responses, regulate cell survival or cell death, and increase inflammation. Zwerling notes that further research needs to be done to see how artificial sweeteners impair signaling and promote inflammation in humans, specifically related to the biomarker pathways associated with Alzheimer’s disease.

In a recent development, the 2025 study raises concern that regular consumption of certain low- and no-calorie sweeteners may be associated with accelerated cognitive decline. However, it does not establish that artificial sweeteners cause neurodegeneration or dementia. Not all artificial sweeteners affect neurotransmitters the same way. “The study highlighted this risk in the younger cohort. Given that artificial sweeteners limit sugary beverages and risk for obesity, further studies are needed as midlife obesity has been associated with risk of cognitive decline,” Zwerling clarifies.

Recent findings suggest that preclinical and computational research has proposed potential inflammatory and molecular pathways through which aspartame could influence biological processes relevant to Alzheimer’s disease. However, these mechanisms have not been established in human studies, and their relevance at typical dietary exposure levels remains uncertain.

The answer depends on several factors, mainly a person’s health history and potential risks. Zwerling says that some sweeteners may influence gut microbiome composition. Others may affect glucose metabolism and insulin responses. She also notes that observational studies have raised questions about cardiovascular and cognitive health. Replacing sugar with non-nutritive sweeteners can reduce caloric and sugar intake, but Zweling cautions that this does not necessarily translate into long-term health benefits.

In a recent development, brief agrees, adding that we shouldn’t automatically label artificial sweeteners as bad, but we also shouldn’t assume that replacing sugar with a zero-calorie alternative automatically makes a product healthier. “Different sweeteners have different properties and potential physiological effects. For someone who regularly consumes sugar-sweetened beverages, switching to an artificially sweetened, lower-calorie, lower-sugar option may be a practical way to reduce added sugar intake,” Brief explains. “Just like everything in nutrition and wellness, this is relative to a person’s individual diet.” She encourages people to gradually reduce their reliance on intensely sweetened foods and beverages and prioritize minimally processed foods. “The goal isn’t to eliminate carbohydrates or naturally occurring sugars, but to be mindful of excessive added sugar intake,” says Brief.

According to Zwerling, no established amount of artificial sweetener has been demonstrated to be optimal for long-term brain health. According to Zweling, certain regulatory agencies have established acceptable daily intake (ADI) levels for individual sweeteners. “These represent amounts considered safe for daily lifetime consumption, not thresholds at which cognitive effects have been ruled out.” She reiterates that excessive added sugar consumption is associated with adverse metabolic health and may indirectly contribute to cognitive decline through insulin resistance, inflammation, and vascular disease.

It has been revealed that she adds that neither excessive sugar nor heavy reliance on artificial sweeteners should substitute for a nutritionally adequate dietary pattern. For brain health, Zweling states a reasonable approach is to minimize excess added sugar and avoid relying heavily on artificial sweeteners as a long-term substitute. A dietary pattern emphasizing whole foods, fruits, vegetables, fiber, and minimally processed foods is preferable. Brief co-signs the advice: “I generally encourage people to avoid excessive reliance on sweeteners and focus on building a diet that doesn’t require everything to taste sweet.” She recommends exploring ways to add natural sweetness without relying heavily on sugar substitutes. “Fresh or frozen fruit, mashed banana, unsweetened applesauce, cinnamon, and vanilla extract are all great options. Honey, maple syrup, coconut sugar, and date syrup are better-for-you, less-processed options that are still sources of added sugar,” says Brief.

Recent findings suggest that beyond the research pool, Zweling adds that work is needed, especially in food desert areas, to ensure these nutritious foods are available. “This emphasizes the need for health providers and patients/caregivers to work with community-based organizations to ensure access to healthy foods,” Zweling stresses. “Brain health is not simply a matter of telling people what to eat; it is also about ensuring they have access to the foods that support healthy aging,” she concludes.

#124362. Lea Michele Wants a Scream Queens Reboot, Too

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1642 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elle ↗ Open Full Page

Lea Michele Wants a Scream Queens Reboot, Too

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • It has been revealed that with multiple projects on the horizon, all eyes are on Lea Michele.
  • According to recent reports, it’s a natural collaboration, as the Bronx-born Michele is the perfect shepherd for a curated NYC experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It has been revealed that with multiple projects on the horizon, all eyes are on Lea Michele. Glee is getting a reboot; fans are begging for Scream Queens to come back, and the actress and singer is about to embark on a tour with Chess co-star Aaron Tveit. She also just starred in Kiehl’s newly introduced “Gift Like a Local” campaign. In partnership with Uber, Michele traveled around to small businesses in New York City and doled out Kiehl’s products. The Glee star even picked most of the stops herself. “Kiehl’s had emailed me and they said, ‘We really want to feature some local businesses in this campaign. Can you send us some of your thoughts?’” she indicates. “It took me about 30 seconds. I had an email with 50 places.”.

According to recent reports, it’s a natural collaboration, as the Bronx-born Michele is the perfect shepherd for a curated NYC experience. In many ways, she breathes New York. She’s starred on Broadway multiple times, most recently in Chess, which just received a Grammy nomination for Best Musical Theater Album. In the later seasons of Glee, her character, Rachel Berry, moved to New York to chase her Broadway dreams (Michele is also rumored to be returning to the show’s reboot). She presently lives in New York with her husband and two children. On the morning of our interview, fresh off a sold-out show with Tveit at the Beacon Theater, she’s having a classic New York morning. “I took my kids to school. I was walking in the sunshine, I had my matcha. I’m getting ready for an event right now,” she notes. “It just is a great day.”.

Below, Michele talks about Glee, her collaboration with Kiehl’s, and whether she’d ever come back for a Scream Queens reboot.

Recent findings suggest that aaron [Tveit] would love my personal favorite, the Grapefruit Body Cleanser. That’s just my tried-and-true. I used it this morning. If you’re feeling a little tired, it helps you to wake up and feel good. But even if you’re not, if you’re feeling like how I felt this morning, energized and happy, it’s just one of my favorite ways to start the day. Love, love, love their body lotion. It’s one of the only body lotions that I feel like actually works for me and helps to really moisturize my skin. They have all these amazing little kits as well over the holidays. I’ve given my dad Kiehl’s lip balm and eye cream in his stockings every year for the holidays.

Sources indicate that I’m really excited to be a part of the Kiehl’s family now. I love our commercial that we shot and the fact that we had the opportunity to support some of the local small businesses.

It has been revealed that I grew up here. I was born in the Bronx. My father owned a deli here in the city. We had ice cream parlors and candy shops. We featured Élan Flowers in my neighborhood. Seasons in Times Square is somewhere that I go all the time and buy flowers for people in Broadway shows. I love Onda, it’s an amazing little facial and wellness store in Tribeca. Obviously, so many little coffee shops. I mean, the list is quite long.

Sources indicate that I just love everything white. I love all-white. My house is all white, but peonies are my favorite flowers. I love hydrangeas. I love white roses. I just love a big white bouquet of flowers.

[Aaron Tveit] and I just found out this morning that almost the entire tour sold out. [It] took less than 24 hours. At our show last night, I think we learned so much about what the show is and what the show could be. We had to cut 10 songs from the concert because we just have so much material. I don’t think that we’re going to do the same show every night. I think that each city is going to get their own show. We’re going to do some of what I would say are our greatest hits together, and some of our individual hits that I think that I will always do in concert, but I really just feel like there’s so much that we can do.

I want Radio City to be epic. We haven’t really talked about having some friends join us, but that’s also something that we could definitely do if we wanted to and bring out some friends to sing some songs with us. The options are endless.

[Aaron is] one of my dearest friends. His wife is one of my closest friends. He’s friends with my husband. Our children are friends. [It’s] amazing that I get to work with someone that I just respect and care about so much.

Sources indicate that it feels awesome. Normally I know when these things are happening, but my publicist texted me in the morning. She was like, “You got a Grammy nomination.” I cried. My reaction was so, even for me, surprising and unexpected. I just broke down. My husband was walking our kids out the door to take them to school, and I was like, “I can’t believe this. We got nominated for a Grammy.” It means so much. I can’t tell you the talent of the cast of Chess. Every single cast member, the most extraordinary talent, our ensemble, the band. To have the cast get this incredible honor, it’s beyond well deserved. I think every single person who saw Chess would agree.

In a recent development, we are constantly one-upping each other in the wellness world. He’ll be like, “Have you seen this? Do you have this?” He had some sort of, I don’t know if it was an infrared mat, and I was like, “Okay, I need that. What’s that?” He saw that I had an amazing water filter in my house, and he’s like, “Okay, what’s that? I need that.” He is probably one of the only people who could rival me in my biohacking, wellness, and taking care of myself.

Most of the time during Chess, if we weren’t talking about Summer House and all of the drama, we were talking about what are all of the wellness things that we’re doing and to try to stay healthy.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been doing Pilates for years. Emma Roberts took me to my first Pilates class when we were living in Upcoming Orleans together, shooting Scream Queens. We went to Romney Studios and did a private lesson. I fell in love with it. Since then, I’ve done mat Pilates and hot Pilates and power Pilates. Everything. I felt pretty good going into this, being like, “I know what I need to know.”.

It wasn’t my first time playing a killer on television, which was also kind of funny. It was so awesome to return to television last night after so many years, and I just had a really great time.

Sources indicate that I met a little girl last night at the meet-and-greet. She was probably 7 years old, and she came to see the concert with her two dads. Her dads were like, “We just are starting to show her some of the musical numbers.” I was like, “Look at you, you’re a little Rachel Berry.” She had her headband on and her cute little penny loafers, and it was just the sweetest thing. What we all created, and what Ryan and Brad and Ian created with Glee, was just so amazing. The things that people say to me about how much it affected their life and brought them so much joy means the world to me.

I hear stories like that from people all the time, and I know that it really means so much to all of us.

It has been revealed that the love for Scream Queens has always been there. Emma [Roberts] and I love that show. We talk about it all the time. Ryan knows, too. Ryan and I talk about it always and I beg him all the time. I’m like, “Can we please bring Scream Queens back?” Ryan should do it. It would be awesome.

It’s so beautiful. I talked a lot about Spring Awakening during my concert last night. We are celebrating 20 years of Spring Awakening opening on Broadway this December. We have a group chat with the original cast. Myself, Lauren Pritchard, and Jonathan Groff are planning a really special private night just for the original cast, a little celebration. I’m so excited that it’s coming to Off-Broadway. My dear, dear, dear sister, Lilli Cooper, is going to be in it. Spring Awakening is such a beautiful and important show, and so anytime that it has the opportunity for people to see it, it should be there. It’s the most beautiful piece of art.

Industry observers note that oh, yeah. I’ve had the opportunity and the real honor to be a part of some incredible original Broadway productions, both with Ragtime and Spring Awakening. It’s an incredible, incredible show.

It has been revealed that there are so many. I want to do everything, I really do. I want to do it all. If I am lucky enough to perform on Broadway for the rest of my life, then that would just be the greatest dream. There are so many great demonstrates that have been on Broadway that could be revived and amazing pieces and incredibly talented artists that are writing original pieces as well. So, I’m ready and available for whatever is to come.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

In a recent development, you’ve got the turkey basted and roasting in the oven. You’ve got your grandmother’s perfect mac and cheese. You’ve got mashed potatoes—the best. Here’s a whiskey sour that makes your fall-flavor dreams come true.

It has been revealed that add ingredients to a shaker and shake without ice. Pour into a glass and garnish with grated nutmeg and a dried apple slice.

This twist on the old-fashioned adds an autumnal flavor that will keep this classic feeling fresh.

Recent findings suggest that combine all ingredients into a mixing glass with ice. Stir until chilled and diluted. Strain into a rocks glass with a large cube. Garnish with an orange peel studded with cloves.

The delicious spice that goes into a pie doesn’t have to be just for lattes or baked goods.

Cover the rim of a stemless wineglass in simple syrup. Dip in cinnamon sugar and add ice to the glass. Pour in pumpkin-spice liqueur and Josh Cellars sauvignon blanc. Stir, then top off the glass with seltzer.

This three-ingredient cocktail is easy to whip up but will taste like it was complicated and time-consuming.

Industry observers note that mix cider and cinnamon whiskey in a Champagne flute. Top with Champagne, then stir lightly until incorporated. Garnish with an apple slice.

A sweet, fizzy sipper to enjoy before dinner.

Sources indicate that add all liquid ingredients to a stemless wineglass. Add ice. Stir to incorporate, then garnish.

A roasty, toasty espresso martini to enjoy after the significant dinner.

This sumptuous hot cocktail makes a great Thanksgiving treat.

Place apples, orange, and cloves in a large pitcher. Drizzle honey over the fruit, then add in apple cider, rum, ginger beer, and white wine. Stir to mix. Top with ice and let chill for 20 minutes before serving. Serve in glasses, including the chunks of fruit.

Whoever invented pouring bourbon into a cup of tea, we want to give you a major hug.

Sources indicate that boil water in a teapot. Steep star anise pod or tea bag inside. Add bourbon, honey, lemon, and Tiki bitters to a mug. Stir. Serve in glass mugs with a spoon and the teapot. To enjoy, pour tea over cocktail base to taste and stir.

This aperitivo is the perfect refreshment before you start serving those heavy Thanksgiving dishes.

Pour Campari and sweet vermouth into a highball glass filled with ice. Top with club soda. Garnish with an orange twist.

It has been revealed that stir the Scotch, vermouth, and bitters well with cracked ice. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass. Garnish with a lemon twist.

Simple enough to whip up in under five minutes, this cocktail has enough Scotch to knock Grandpa under the table.

Recent findings suggest that stir the Scotch and amaretto well with cracked ice in a mixing glass. Strain over fresh ice into an old-fashioned glass.

If you’re a big fan of cranberry sauce (the one that comes in a can), you can cure your cranberry craving with this vodka cocktail.

Shake ingredients in a shaker with cracked ice. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass, then garnish with lime.

This green-tinged cocktail tastes fresh and slightly tart, but it’s boozy enough to chill you out after that heavy holiday meal.

The Black Russian is the espresso martini’s cooler, more laid-back cousin. It’s so simple to make and yet deliciously complex in taste.

Industry observers note that stir ingredients with ice in a mixing glass. Strain into an old-fashioned glass over fresh ice.

In a recent development, sometimes you don’t want to have to choose between two options, because you want to have it all! And you can have it both ways, with this gin-and-vodka martini, the vesper.

It has been revealed that stir ingredients briskly with ice in a mixing tin until very cold. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass. Garnish with a large, thin-cut lemon peel.

Why not turn your holiday gathering into an international experience? Incorporate this Russian classic into your cocktail rotation.

Squeeze lime juice into a copper mug (or a Collins glass) and drop in the spent hull. Add ice cubes, then pour in the vodka and fill with cold ginger beer. Serve with a stirring rod.

This rum cocktail will bring back fond memories of warmer weather.

Fill a tall glass with ice cubes. Add rum. Pour in ginger beer and lime juice. Stir with a barspoon, then garnish with a lime wedge.

Holidays are synonymous with Champagne, so pop open a bottle of bubbly and pour out one of these delicious cocktails.

In a recent development, stir rum, lime juice, and honey thoroughly with cracked ice in a chilled cocktail shaker. Pour unstrained into a Collins glass. Top with Champagne.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The allure of soft, understated nails is going nowhere. Rather, throughout 2026, we’ve seen the minimalist manicure movement gain momentum with each new season. “It’s the biggest shift I’ve seen in my chair this year,” indicates celebrity nail technician Iram Shelton. She explains that the theme has been “natural nails, but better,” which is centered around low-maintenance colors and finishes.

It has been revealed that for winter, this translates to sheer, milky tones, short, considered nail shapes and microvariations of wearable nail art. In preparation for party season, expect to see minuscule flecks of metallic gold and star-themed motifs, too. While milky pink nails will always be in style, this winter, it’s all about unexpected sheers like lavender, bronze, and pearly white. Not only do these colors go with everything, but they also are extremely forgiving—you can paint them on yourself without a problem.

Zoya Lavender Perfector Nail Polish.

Londontown Illuminating Nail Concealer in Bare.

Essie Gel Couture Long-Lasting Nail Polish in Liquid Diamonds.

Below, find 10 of the most polished, pared-back nail ideas to bookmark for your next appointment.

Last season, we had Hailey Bieber milk nails, followed by Sienna Miller’s ‘Chantilly cream’. Now? Lavender takes the spotlight, in its dreamiest, near-translucent form. A high-shine top coat makes this tone appear even hazier in the light.

Sources indicate that leaning into minimalism doesn’t necessarily mean forgoing color. Take this rich, berry red for proof; when an all-over pigment isn’t on the cards, a sleek micro French tip is equally flattering.

In a recent development, for a simpler take on autumn’s ‘gold fairy dust’ nail trend (as seen on Taylor Swift), draw inspiration from stardust instead. Here, a natural blushed pink base sits beautifully under a gently dazzling, golden shimmer top coat.

Industry observers note that traditional French tips are given a modern, metallic upgrade without veering into futuristic territory. When reserved for the base of the nail, a gold-toned cuff is eye-catching but in a subtle way.

Sources indicate that frosted pearlescent finishes are as luminous as they are delicate—not to mention destined for winter weather. When worn with a cozy cashmere knit, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more perfect pairing.

Industry observers note that square and squoval nails are seeing a revival this season. Keep your shapes cropped, softly rounded, and ultra-glossy if committing to minimalism.

Recent findings suggest that trade in winter's deep, vibrant mocha, espresso, and cocoa-inspired browns for a sheer bronze pigment. When kept close to the natural nail color, this shade is the best way to embrace elevated color without going overboard.

Industry observers note that while the notion of nail art might suggest something elaborate colorful, petite star motifs make a case for the opposite. One on each nail balances a feeling of festivity with practicality for everyday wear.

Granted, a white Christmas might be far on the horizon. But this set sees micro polka dots get a dainty, wintry upgrade, inspired by tiny droplets of snow.

According to recent reports, if a micro French isn’t your style, an ombré is worth considering. Begin with a nude beige-pink base color, and watch it blend seamlessly into a cozy, seasonal color.

#124355. 9 Interior Trends Designers Are Officially Ditching in 2027

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1505 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

9 Interior Trends Designers Are Officially Ditching in 2027

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the end of the year is a great time to look back and reflect.
  • We love predicting what’s going to be hot in home design for the upcoming seasons; however, you can’t talk about what’s going to be “in” without also touching on what’s going to be “out.” We asked a handful of designers to share what design choices and interior trends they saw a lot of in 2026 that they’re more than happy to leave behind in 2027.
  • We spend so much time making our interiors warm and reflective of our personalities, it would be a shame to ruin the look of these spaces by opting for one-dimensional lighting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the end of the year is a great time to look back and reflect. When it comes to home design, there’s a lot to cover, from fresh trends to furniture collaboration drops to specific internet-breaking interiors. One of our favorite things to do around this time is figure out what’s coming next in terms of interiors.

We love predicting what’s going to be hot in home design for the upcoming seasons; however, you can’t talk about what’s going to be “in” without also touching on what’s going to be “out.” We asked a handful of designers to share what design choices and interior trends they saw a lot of in 2026 that they’re more than happy to leave behind in 2027. Keep reading to find out the nine things they remarked.

We spend so much time making our interiors warm and reflective of our personalities, it would be a shame to ruin the look of these spaces by opting for one-dimensional lighting.

It has been revealed that “It's time to move beyond relying on a single overhead fixture or wall-to-wall recessed lighting to illuminate an entire room,” designer Kristen Mendoza of Four Brothers Design + Build states. “Flat, overly bright lighting can make even the most beautifully designed spaces feel sterile and uninviting.”.

Industry observers note that instead, incorporating layers of lighting to add dimension and create a warm atmosphere is much better for your home. Sconces, picture lights, table lamps, and thoughtfully placed accent lighting at various heights throughout the room, Mendoza adds, give a space a more intimate touch.

In a recent development, “I also recommend using warm 2700K light sources on dimmers to flatter people, highlight architectural details, and bring out the natural beauty of materials,” she explains. “Lighting should be considered early in the design and construction process, not treated as an afterthought.”.

Part of the appeal of “grandma chic” decor is that it’s been collected over time. The pieces show their age, the interior is imperfect, and it’s very clearly reflective of the homeowner’s personality and life. However, “there is a difference between a room that feels ‘collected over time’ and one that feels inherited all at once,” designer Stephanie Kraus explains, and she’s tired of seeing this false presentation on display in people’s homes.

Industry observers note that “Heavy Roman shades with lots of fabric, chintz on top of chintz on top of chintz, fringe on every edge, etc.,” she adds. “One of these details in a room can be charming, but if you use them all together, the room can start to feel like a period movie set.”.

Industry observers note that it’s often clear when this eccentric aesthetic is manufactured rather than effortless. Instead of trying to make the “ideal” interior in the span of a month, be patient and work on your home over a greater span of time. That way, the end product will look authentic.

According to recent reports, though curved sofas are massively popular right now and look gorgeous in a photograph, Kraus is ready to leave them in 2026. “A curved sofa rarely seats more than two people comfortably,” she says. “Once guests settle in, everyone ends up sitting awkwardly, and conversation feels harder than it should.”.

She’s all for a sofa or couch being something that invites people in to linger over conversations and stay late into the night, and a kidney-shaped seat isn’t going to do that.

While designer Maggie Vollrath of Provision Studios loved seeing the return of decorative, playful details like ruffles and scalloped edges, she thinks we’ve gone a bit overboard in 2026. These touches are being applied to just about everything: upholstery, pillows, lampshades, bedding, furniture—the list could go on.

“These details can be incredibly charming, but when they're repeated throughout an entire room, they begin to lose the very character that makes them special,” she claims.

Rather than treat every piece of a room with one of these details, Vollrath suggests opting for a scalloped lampshade or a beautifully tailored ruffled pillow instead to still capture that charm without drowning the space in them.

It has been revealed that “Limiting these details to one or two thoughtful applications allows them to feel intentional rather than overly thematic,” she adds. “Sometimes, the most interesting interiors are as much about what you choose to leave out as what you include.”.

Sources indicate that “I'd love to see us move away from selecting materials simply because they imitate the appearance of something more expensive,” Vollrath explains. This goes beyond marble-printed contact paper and burl wood veneer; the designer means on a larger scale, like mass-produced tile that’s made to replicate the imperfections of handmade zellige.

“Part of what makes authentic zellige so beautiful is the craftsmanship and natural variation that comes from its production,” she says. “When those qualities are artificially reproduced, I think we sometimes lose the very thing that made the original material special.”.

She would rather see a greater appreciation for beautiful, honest materials at every price point, and if the exact thing a homeowner wants is out of budget, then her solution would be to pivot the idea altogether rather than find something cheaply made that looks like what they desire.

“A classic Carrara marble paired with beautifully considered cabinetry can create an incredibly sophisticated interior, even when something as dramatic as Calacatta Viola isn't within the budget,” Vollrath explains.

We could probably say this every year, but it bears repeating: Don’t solely follow trends! “Just because something is trending doesn't mean it's right for your home,” designer Drew Michael Scott of Lone Fox indicates. “Polka dots are having a moment right now, but they don't make sense in many homes, or dare I say, most homes.”.

In a recent development, he suggests thinking of home trends as prompts that should get you to brainstorm fresh ideas for your space that actually fit your style. Take polka dots again. If you want to introduce a new pattern to your home, but you don’t particularly mesh with polka dots, try a stripe instead.

Sources indicate that “If you try to force something you don't love into your home just because it's trending, you're going to drive yourself crazy,” he adds. Let’s leave this line of thinking back in 2026 once and for all.

According to recent reports, while we love a good built-in bookshelf and wooden ceiling beam, those types of architectural details don’t always make sense in every single home. In 2026, as personality-filled interiors became more popular for everyone, a lot of homeowners looked into adding this type of millwork to their spaces as a way to add more visual interest and texture.

“Decorative beams, arches, and elaborate millwork can feel forced when they don't make sense with the architecture of the home,” designer Dani Flax of Pearson Design Group argues. “I think there's a tendency to add these elements to make a space feel more interesting, but the result can actually take away from the architecture itself.”.

A home in a modern farmhouse style, for example, would look a bit odd with an intricate ceiling medallion and excessive picture frame molding. Design your interior around the existing architecture and the style of your home, don’t incorporate these elements simply because they’re everywhere right now.

The next year is not about playing it safe with your interiors—designers are tired of the stark white home. While ubiquitous gray and white color schemes had their time, they can often make a home feel generic and devoid of character.

“In their place, we're embracing more intentional, tonal palettes and color drenching,” Mendoza states.

You can still have a mostly white house, of course, but take a little risk and mix in some pops of color and pattern here and there, or choose a beautiful neutral wood tone for your cabinetry instead of a bright white paint.

“Taking a considered color, whether it's a deep green, warm clay, or earthy mushroom, and carrying it across walls, trim, and cabinetry creates a cohesive, enveloping effect,” Mendoza adds. “The goal isn't necessarily to introduce more color, but to use it with greater confidence and purpose.”.

Sources indicate that this is definitely a hot take, but designer John Maloney McNamara of Coosa Interiors is ready to leave velvet upholstery behind. “I’ve tried, but velvet almost always reads as either a 1990s prom limo or a hotel lobby trying very hard,” he explains. “The sheen shows every crush and bruise, and it ages into something that looks tired rather than loved.”.

In a recent development, if you love the look of velvet, he suggests going with a mohair fabric instead, saying it has all of velvet’s depth and none of its shine. It also only gets better with age. And though he knows creamy bouclé has been overdone, Maloney McNamara thinks it deserves a reprise, but only in a rich color that can replace velvet still.

The Wake Forest-Georgia Tech game on November 21 may have been underwhelming, but it still got plenty of people talking, thanks to a viral moment captured between two students in the stands. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Content warning: This story contains religious slurs and details about sexual and religious abuse.

Industry observers note that I was violated by a group of strangers who took turns stripping me of my hijab. It started with them exposing my hair and making hateful remarks about the hijab. Then it quickly escalated. They removed my clothes to expose my body. They wrote degrading words on me. They encouraged each other. My protests only made them do it more.

It started out as an otherwise happy moment for me. I was attending the historic inauguration of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and celebrating the first Muslim mayor in Upcoming York City’s history. It was an occasion being celebrated by not just New Yorkers but also fellow Americans and people around the world for the symbol of increasing visibility and inclusion that the moment represented for so many of us. I snapped a quick selfie in front of the stage with the inauguration banner billowing behind me.

Recent findings suggest that in the selfie, I’m bundled up in a burgundy fur-trimmed coat, my hijab clinging to my head against the cold winter wind. I’m proudly smiling at the camera. Despite the cold, I’m so happy. It was this photo, uploaded to my X account, that users prompted Grok to regenerate in rapid succession in ways that violated my consent and religious autonomy. They used an AI chatbot to digitally take control of my body to inflict their abuse.

“I’ve always wondered what you all whackos look like without all that mess.”.

I founded Muslim Girl, a digital media platform, as a teenager to reclaim our narratives and identities online. I wanted Muslim women to speak for ourselves, on our own terms, instead of allowing others to define us. I’ve dedicated my career to empowering women to take control of their own choices. But in a matter of moments, Grok robbed me of mine.

Industry observers note that elon Musk, the owner of xAI, essentially removed all the guardrails from Grok to compete in the AI race. By allowing Grok’s image generation feature to remove clothing and promote its “spicy” capabilities, Musk was banking on consumers using it for sexual purposes without any regard to the harms it would cause.

The person I was most afraid to tell was my dad. After my mom passed away a few years ago, he’s become way more protective of his only daughter, and for an old-school Arab Muslim immigrant, I didn’t know how he would react. He was furious. At first, I was afraid he was going to be mad at me for being in this situation since I have always been a vocally public woman online. But he understood very swiftly that technology was being used to inflict the same abuse I had gotten used to online in more advanced and extreme ways.

Most of my elders don’t know the difference between AI-generated images and real photos, especially those who habitually forward chain messages in massive WhatsApp family group chats. My dad had to figure out a way to preemptively and sensitively explain to them what happened. Even though the images weren’t technically real, the humiliation of having to explain them to family and friends remained the same.

Industry observers note that coming from a religiously conservative background heightened the feeling of violation I experienced. The hijab is meant to be a woman’s choice. I’ve worn mine since I was 13 years old, so no public photos of me exist without me wearing it. I wear the hijab not out of heightened strictness or chastity, but rather as a guard against the male gaze in a hypersexualized society that commodifies women’s bodies and pressures us into how we should look or present ourselves.

Once the choice to cover or uncover is taken from a woman, it can easily become a tool of control and dominance over her body. In France, we’ve seen the proposal of a hijab ban that would fine women for covering, at the same time as we’ve watched countries like Afghanistan force women to cover. In all cases, the point is asserting power over women’s bodies.

Technology has created upcoming ways to violate our autonomy while our current laws struggle to keep pace with protecting our rights in the AI era. Our bodies are still a battleground. Only now, the battleground is digital.

When the notifications started pouring in, I didn’t know what to do against the faceless mob that was using Grok to replicate and violate my identity in such shocking ways. I called the police, and when they came over, I had to endure the first humiliating experience of showing them the photos. They took a police report, noted there was nothing they could do, and suggested that I make my account private. I refuse to diminish myself from the public at risk of having my basic rights and dignity violated online. None of us should have to.

That’s why I’m suing Elon Musk’s xAI. This isn’t just about my hijab or even about me. It’s about what we will and will not allow AI to do to us. I hope this becomes a landmark case that draws a line for the rights we are entitled to online. Even if it means standing up to the richest man on Earth.

#124335. The Inconvenient Truth About the Electricity AI Requires

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

The Inconvenient Truth About the Electricity AI Requires

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • He-Man liked to exclaim: “I have the power!” AI should be so lucky.
  • When it comes to the wielders of artificial intelligence, and the data centers needed to fuel it, language and numbers become inescapably extreme: trillions in investment, gigawatts of electricity, the extinction of the human race.
  • grid is not designed for large data-center loads,” claims Anubhav Arora, senior director of global infrastructure at Fitch and a coauthor of a recent paper the ratings agency published on data centers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

He-Man liked to exclaim: “I have the power!” AI should be so lucky.

When it comes to the wielders of artificial intelligence, and the data centers needed to fuel it, language and numbers become inescapably extreme: trillions in investment, gigawatts of electricity, the extinction of the human race. It’s almost cartoonish, until you get down to some brass tacks: The power is not there to fuel these dreams of the would-be Masters of the Universe.

“The U.S. grid is not designed for large data-center loads,” claims Anubhav Arora, senior director of global infrastructure at Fitch and a coauthor of a recent paper the ratings agency published on data centers. “Securing reliable, sufficient power is the single greatest bottleneck in data-center development,” the paper’s authors write. (Esquire and Fitch share the same parent manufacturer, Hearst.).

In the U.S.—which is by far the world leader in data centers—electricity demand from the facilities could reach up to 649 terawatt-hours (TWh) a year by 2030, according to a 2026 Berkeley Lab analysis, or roughly 12 percent of all U.S. electricity consumption. Powering New York City for an entire year requires one tenth that energy.

According to recent reports, meeting global demand for compute could require nearly $7 trillion in capital investment by 2030, including $5.2 trillion for AI-related data centers, according to McKinsey estimates. Estimates from Goldman Sachs Research say that Europe will need to invest more than $3.5 trillion on its grid in the next ten years to cope with increased demand. (China looks to be fine, but it is slow to the data-center boom.).

In a recent development, and the problem is not just a lack of juice. “The actual grid infrastructure . . . is also basically limited in terms of transmission capacity, and the interconnection process is a little bit outdated,” indicates Arora. That grid—the network of transmission lines, transformers, and power plants that create and distribute electricity to hundreds of millions of users—is constrained, and the interconnection backlog is massive. Put another way: Not only is the shop running low on milk, but the line to get inside is stretching around the block. “You could build a data center in one and a half to two years, but to get interconnection, it takes five to ten years,” Arora says.

According to recent reports, according to Cleanview, a tech giant that tracks U.S. power infrastructure, there are currently 1,454 operating data centers, as well as up to 578 under construction and 2,663 proposed. Companies like Alphabet, Meta, and Anthropic are scrambling. With that scramble, there is money to be made. PJM, the largest power-grid operator in the United States, has been trying to devise a latest way to accommodate the data-center boom. Its proposed “Bring Your Own New Capacity” (or BYONC) framework would have allowed new data-center projects to buy energy in the form of a battery and add it to the grid. But in October, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission rejected that portion of PJM’s proposal, sending the grid operator back to the drawing board.

Industry observers note that notable here is what kind of data centers we’re talking about. Of the more than 3,200 data centers proposed globally, 800 of them are hyperscalers. These are the biggies. The campuses. Sprawling centers with square footage in the millions and power demands upwards of 100 MW (which could power 100,000 homes). Collectively, some estimates put the global power usage at 200 TWh annually. (That’s juice for 11 million homes.).

How can companies even think about the grid beginning to handle that demand? Increasingly, they aren’t. Many hyperscalers are looking to “bring your own power [BYOP],” states Jonathon Smith, associate director of Sustainable Finance Research at Fitch. In other words, build their own power plants. The problem here is twofold: First, very few people on the planet know how to build something like this. You could buy the biggest army the world has ever seen; try moving it without engineers. Second, it poses very real and very dangerous environmental threats.

Recently, the journal Nature Sustainability published a study revealing that the annual carbon dioxide emissions of the largest data centers in the U.S. are equal to that of a small country, like Paraguay or Denmark. And that study looked at data centers from 2024 and 2025. Data centers have exploded since then, with as much as a 190 percent increase from 2025 to 2026.

When companies like Anthropic say, “Don’t worry, we’re not even touching the grid,” it brings up a cartoon situation more akin to The Simpsons than a Saturday-morning serial. Picture it: a giant data center, clean, cool, not an emission in sight, just humming machines and maybe a security guard. But there’s a pipe going out the back, and if you follow it as it snakes around the corner, it connects to a behemoth power plant, burning enough natural gas to power a city, with plumes of smoke assaulting the sky above. Animated, but closer to the reality of BYOP.

“From an environmental-impact perspective, most of these developers are deploying natural-gas-based assets for power, which release GHG [greenhouse gas] emissions and air pollutants,” notes Smith. The cleaner alternatives are renewables (unlikely), nuclear (terrifying), and batteries (no environmental picnic, either).

Industry observers note that among the environmental concerns—which inevitably bleed into the social and economic ones—are these centers’ use of water, which they need in great volume to keep those humming stacks of servers cool. While many experts point to these complications as overblown, especially as data centers look to closed-loop systems (there is an initial dump of water that gets cooled and reused), the reason you won’t stop hearing about water use is because 1) it’s concerning, and 2) water is inherently political and always has been. (Traditionally, we’ve needed the stuff to feed our animals, grow our crops, and, you know, live.) Go back to the early chapters of the Bible and what’s causing strife? Water. Go back even further and some of the first wars ever recorded—4,500 years ago in ancient Sumeria—are over the stuff. And data centers have become a fast-moving political football.

Sources indicate that A recent Gallup poll indicates that 71 percent of Americans do not want an AI data center near where they live. Those are some very substantial numbers. It’s vital to clarify that the data centers big tech wants to build near dense populations are for cloud computing, and they make up roughly 70 percent of all data centers. While centers for AI computing and AI training are catching up, these can be built farther away, for the simple reason that we’re happy to wait a few minutes for AI to do our taxes but not for the cloud to recombobulate an email or Instagram post.

Sources indicate that that’s still a huge number of data centers that need to be near you and me, so what will we do about it? The politicians are listening. New York State has issued a moratorium. There’s legislation limiting the centers on the table in nine other states. Gina Hinojosa, who just pummeled Greg Abbott in the Governor's race in Texas, campaigned on promises of a moratorium for permitting and construction on new data centers. Norway, the Netherlands, and Denmark are leading the charge on moratoriums and other restrictions in Europe as governments catch up with popular opinion.

Moreover, back in the U.S.A., Donald Trump has touted a “deal” with massive tech on data centers, the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, supposedly protecting grids from the biggies. But never has Tip O’Neill’s maxim that “All politics is local” been more salient. More than 500 localities are forming their own moratoriums, zoning freezes, and permit pauses. Even after the midterms, how and if to move forward with data centers is a debate for states, counties, cities, townships, and any other geographic entity that makes laws, collects taxes, and breathes collective air.

As the Democrats take over Congress and data centers become every pol’s favorite newly introduced cudgel, as the European Union and member states enact regulatory frameworks (often tied to renewable energy and climate), as elected officials turn away from AI’s once sunnily vague promises, something is becoming clear: It’s humans who have the power.
